summary:
Ayush Bhardwaj frames his talk around building and iterating applied vertical AI systems, drawing parallel experience from a hedge fund and a pharma tech startup. He defines applied vertical AI as AI built for one specific industry job, contrasting general-purpose tools like Google Translate with narrow products like Elos for drug work. Despite cultural differences between industries, he found the applied AI workflow identical and the same obstacles reappearing across legal and proptech as well.

He rejects the common question of whether agents reach production, arguing the real question is whether they make or save money end-to-end. His seven-step recipe begins with formulating a narrow task, then identifying proprietary data, modeling the prompt after the target expert, adding observability, and hiring the user. The first four steps fit on one screen and are not a moat; proprietary data and the domain expert are.

The hard part is iteration. Engineers can spot bad code instantly but cannot judge a trade thesis or a drug candidate. He describes trying and failing to use an LLM as a judge, because models merely jargon their way through domains like alpha. Verifiable rewards work for math and code but not these fields. The training data is structurally withheld: hedge fund holdings disclosures destroy returns, and roughly 30% of pharma firms fail to disclose trial outcomes, which the FDA reminded 2,000 sponsors about in 2026. Frontier labs therefore lack this data, and experts cannot annotate cheaply due to NDAs.

His answer is to hire the user and build a learning loop around them. The expert curates sources, refines prompts, decomposes problems into a logical flow, and judges outputs. Starting from the cheapest rung, error analysis on observability logs, the team gradually climbs toward supervised fine-tuning, rubrics-as-rewards, and ultimately RLHF. Pitfalls include echo-chamber feedback with rubric rewards and the cost of re-fine-tuning when base models like GLM 5.2, Deep Seek, or others update. The loop expands as more users generate proprietary data.

He reframes HITL as AITL for finance and pharma: AI proposes candidates, but the trader or scientist still decides. Models today do correlation, not causation, so vibe-coded drugs and markets remain future possibilities. His final takeaway: model and infra are commodities; domain expertise and curated proprietary data are the only moat.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Production deployment is not the right question; ROI and end-to-end value are.
Iteration is the bottleneck, not building the agent or the prompt.
LLM-as-a-judge fails in niche verticals because the model lacks domain instincts and just predicts probable jargon.
Proprietary data is the only moat; models and infrastructure are commodities.
In finance and pharma, the most useful training data is structurally withheld for competitive and legal reasons.

Climb the learning ladder from error analysis, to rubrics-as-rewards, to supervised fine-tuning, to RLHF, while being wary of rubric echo chambers.

sections.title: Reading the room and speaker intro
sections.summary: Bhardwaj introduces himself as an applied AI engineer from a hedge fund now doing everything tech plus AI at a pharma tech startup. He polls the audience for engineers vs. people managers, joking that managing AI agents does not count.

sections.title: What applied vertical AI actually means
sections.summary: He coins and defines applied vertical AI: applied AI built for one specific industry to simulate a job in that industry. He contrasts Google Translate with Elos for drug work, and cites legal tech as another vertical example.

sections.title: Leaving a hedge fund for pharma and changing nothing
sections.summary: He expected a culture change between fast hedge fund work and slow, deliberate pharma work, but found his core applied AI job unchanged. He observed the same pattern in legal AI and proptech, suggesting an abstractable recipe.

sections.title: The wrong question about agents in production
sections.summary: He reframes the common question from 'are agents in production' to whether they actually work, justify ROI, and make or save more money than invested, confirming yes from both his workplaces.

sections.title: Step one, make the task narrow
sections.summary: Step one is formulating a narrow problem. He gives a finance example of ranking US IT equities by specific parameters rather than asking for top market opportunities, and notes pharma workflows get the same step-by-step decomposition.

sections.title: Proprietary data is the only real differentiator
sections.summary: Step two is identifying proprietary data. Public news, sell-side reports, arXiv, and PubMed are available to everyone. Finance trade theses and pharma failed-experiment data are expensive, hard to buy, and must be curated, often by converting unstructured internal data with LLM workflows.

sections.title: The easy part fits on one screen
sections.summary: Steps three and four, prompt modeling after the target person and observability with traces for debugging, are trivial. The entire foundation fits on one screen, so it is not a moat; only proprietary data is.

sections.title: Why you cannot iterate on what you cannot judge
sections.summary: He could build the agent but could not judge whether it worked because he lacks training as a trader or biologist. Engineers instantly spot bad code, but lack that mental model for trade theses or drug candidates. This is where vertical AI projects silently die.

sections.title: Trying to use a model as the judge
sections.summary: He attempted LLM-as-a-judge, calling it a stupid mistake. Models just predict the next probable word and jargon their way through without understanding domain terms like alpha, whereas a human instantly knows what is and isn't.

sections.title: The data was never there, by design
sections.summary: Models cannot verify themselves in these fields because RLVR needs answer keys. Worse, finance and pharma structurally withhold training data: hedge fund holdings filings above $100M drop returns once reverse-engineered, and ~30% of pharma firms never disclose trial outcomes, prompting FDA reminders to ~2,000 sponsors in 2026. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has this data, and traders cannot be hired at $100/hour to annotate due to NDAs.

sections.title: Hire the user
sections.summary: After enumerating problems, he concludes the answer is to hire the person you want to sell to, because there is no other way around.

sections.title: Hiring in practice and the payoff
sections.summary: In the hedge fund the user was his boss, the trader. At the pharma startup, hiring a 20-year scientist felt odd for young engineers but changed the trajectory of the tools. Pitching to big pharma, the tools started speaking their language rather than jargon.

sections.title: Building the learning loop around a domain expert
sections.summary: The expert helps at the lowest level by curating sources, refining prompts, and decomposing problems into a natural five-step flow before finally judging. Their lived judgment turns into the agent. Multiple techniques exist: supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, rubrics-as-rewards (which he calls RLAIF but warns can create echo chambers), and error analysis on observability logs, which is the cheapest and highest ROI starting point. From there teams climb to SFT and ultimately RLHF.

sections.title: Pitfalls and the self-reinforcing data loop
sections.summary: Re-fine-tuning is required as base models like GLM 5.2 or Deep Seek release newer versions, adding cost. Once the loop runs, hiring more users increases queries, scope, and proprietary data generated by the workflow itself. The loop never stops until the product is shipped to paying users.

sections.title: Justifying ROI in finance and pharma
sections.summary: Citing the Stanford AI Index, he notes 80-89% of enterprise AI agents never reach production, but he reframes this as failure to justify cost rather than failure to ship. These verticals will not wait 2-3 years; the product must hit the ground running and instantly make money.

sections.title: The seven steps summarized
sections.summary: He recaps: formulate the problem, source data, prompt well, observe performance, hire the user, form the endless learning loop, and ship once the tool delivers alpha over Claude or ChatGPT.

sections.title: AITL not HITL, and the AGI line
sections.summary: HITL is premature for finance and pharma; instead, AI is in the loop, proposing candidates while the trader or scientist still decides. Models today do correlation, not causation, so vibe-coded drugs and markets remain future possibilities, gated by what he calls the AGI line.

sections.title: Final takeaway: domain expertise and data are the moat
sections.summary: Model and infra ecosystems are commodities sold by every vendor at the conference. The moat that no one will sell you is domain expertise plus proprietary data not available on the open internet. He thanks the audience and invites questions.

organization.name: Allos AI
organization.summary: Allos AI is an independent Oxford-area pharmaceutical technology company that builds a glass-box causal AI platform for complex drug reformulation. First-party pages describe simulation-led design of experiments, validated operating windows, version-controlled tech transfer, and clinical-trial support using real-world data. The January 2026 Allos press release announced $5 million in seed financing led by Oxford Science Enterprises to commercialize the platform. Ayush Bhardwaj is Tech Lead; the talk’s “Elos” / pharma-tech employer is this company.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage, about, and AI platform pages are live. $5M seed announced 2026-01-12. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
